description: Width tiers for HASS Year 2 — ACARA v9. One entry per descriptor. K-strand descriptors use phenomena_contexts; S-strand descriptors use task_contexts.
subject: HASS

width_notes.minimum_width: For K-strand (Knowledge) descriptors: the narrowest set of phenomena or contexts that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For S-strand (Skills/Inquiry) descriptors: the narrowest task context in which the skill is applied — one source type, one inquiry topic, one representation format.
width_notes.typical_width: For K-strand descriptors: engagement across the elaboration range. For S-strand descriptors: the skill practised across two or more task types or source contexts representative of the elaboration scope.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new phenomena, cultural contexts, or task contexts. First Nations elaborations always appear in wider where present in ACARA source material.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations used as source data. First Nations elaborations consistently placed in wider.

AC9HS2K01.minimum_width: Investigate one local individual, group, place or building and identify reasons for their importance.
AC9HS2K01.typical_width: Investigate a range of locally significant people, buildings and sites; describe their social, cultural or heritage significance to present and past generations; explain why significance can vary across community groups.
wider: Identify and explore local sites and landscapes of significance to First Nations Australians — for example, engraving sites, rock paintings, natural features — and compare the nature of their significance with that of heritage-listed built structures
Design a local historical tour of a significant building or site, identifying which community groups attach significance to it and why their reasons may differ
elaborations: suggesting reasons for the location of a local landmark before searching for resources that provide an explanation; for example, community building, statue or war memorial

investigating the history of a chosen person, building, site or place in the local community, using provided sources (for example, the internet, books, newspapers, community information guides, audio-visual material, digital sources, photographs) and relating a story that these reveal about the past

discussing why a particular site has heritage significance or cultural value for present generations; for example, it provides a record of a significant historical event, has aesthetic value, reflects the community's identity

identifying and visiting, where appropriate, local sites, places and landscapes of significance to First Nations Australians; for example, engraving sites, rock paintings, natural sites or features such as the creeks or mountains
identifying and designing a local historical tour of a building or site; for example, one related to a particular cultural group

AC9HS2K02.minimum_width: Identify one technological development and describe how it changed people's daily lives.
AC9HS2K02.typical_width: Examine changes across multiple technology types — transport, communication, household technologies — across generations; explain how these changes shaped patterns of work, travel and daily life.
wider: Investigate the technologies used by local First Nations Australians for food, shelter and transportation, and consider how these technologies reflect deep knowledge of local environments

Explore how current communication and transport technologies connect people to distant places, comparing the range of places accessible now with what would have been accessible one or two generations ago
elaborations: examining changes in technologies over several generations by comparing past and present objects and photographs, and discussing how these changes have shaped people's lives; for example, changes to land, air and sea transport; the introduction of transistors, television, FM radio moving to digital streaming, including how people communicated over long distances
identifying, through questioning adults, the communication, work and transport technologies used in the childhoods of their grandparents or familiar elders
suggesting what their pattern of visits to places might have been one or two generations ago and comparing this to their current pattern
identifying the technologies used by local First Nations Australians for aspects of daily life such as providing food, shelter and transportation

identifying the ways current communication and transport technologies impact on our interconnections with other places; for example, online communication, accessibility to other places through different types of transport

AC9HS2K03.minimum_width: Identify where they live in Australia relative to their nearest capital city on a map.
AC9HS2K03.typical_width: Locate their place within Australia across local, regional and state/territory scales on maps and a globe; describe how people and places are interconnected — through shopping, recreation, family visits — across those scales.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' songlines connect places across large distances, comparing this way of representing spatial interconnection with a conventional road or transport map
Explore how communication and transport technologies connect their local place to regional and state/territory places, tracing specific goods, services or people across those connections
elaborations: identifying where they live in Australia, including in relation to their nearest capital city, the region and state/territory on a map and a globe
investigating the places locally and at a broader scale that they and their families visit for shopping, health, recreation, religious or ceremonial activities, or other reasons

identifying links they and other people in their community have with people and places at the regional and/or state/territory scale; for example, where produce in their supermarket comes from or produce from their farms goes to, relatives they visit, places they go for holidays

describing how communication and transport technologies connect their place to other places at the regional and/or state/territory level; for example, online communication, phone, road, rail, planes, ferries

AC9HS2K04.minimum_width: Identify the First Nations Australians' language group connected to the local area and describe one way they are interconnected with Country/Place.
AC9HS2K04.typical_width: Explore the relationship between a local First Nations language group and their Country/Place — including connections to land, sea, waterways, sky and animals; discuss when and how Acknowledgement of Country and Welcome to Country are used appropriately.
wider: Investigate the relationship between language, Country/Place and spirituality for the local First Nations language group, exploring how language itself encodes knowledge of Country/Place
Compare how two different First Nations communities (local and a contrasting group from another region) express their connections to Country/Place through stories, songs or ceremonies
elaborations: listening to stories connecting local First Nations Australians with the land, sea, waterways, sky and animals of their Country/Place

liaising with community to identify language groups of First Nations Australians who belong to the local area and exploring the relationship between language, Country/Place and spirituality (this is intended to be a local area study with a focus on one language group; however, if information or sources are not readily available, another representative area may be studied)

discussing when to use Acknowledgement of Country and Welcome to Country at ceremonies and events to respectfully recognise the Country/Place and Traditional Owners and Custodians of the land, sea, waterways, and sky

AC9HS2S01.minimum_width: Develop at least one inquiry question about a historical site or place using a provided question stem.
AC9HS2S01.typical_width: Develop inquiry questions about historical sites and places across multiple dimensions — physical features, purpose, change over time, personal connection; use a range of question stems including 'How do I feel about…?' and 'What effect…?'
wider: Generate questions that probe why a place or event is significant to different groups — including First Nations Australians — rather than only asking factual 'what' and 'where' questions
Develop questions independently before, during and after an investigation, demonstrating ongoing inquiry rather than front-loaded questioning only
elaborations: developing inquiry questions about a historical site; for example, "What does it look like now?", "What condition is it in?", "What was its purpose?", "How might its use have changed?", "How was it built/created?", "Who built it?", "How is it now used?", "Why is it important?", "Was/is it used by different groups of people?"

developing inquiry questions about places; for example, "What are the features of the place?", "How far away is it?", "How easy is it to get to?", "How am I connected to it?", "How is it connected to other places?"
posing questions using the stems, "How do I feel about …?", 'What would it be like to …?" and "What effect …?"

AC9HS2S02.minimum_width: Collect and record information from one provided source type and locate one connected place on a map.
AC9HS2S02.typical_width: Collect information from multiple source types (photographs, interviews, satellite images, maps, observations of heritage sites); create annotated pictorial maps with symbols; order key events in unscaled timelines.
wider: Collect information from field observations and archival sources about the same place or event, comparing what each reveals and recording findings in a combined annotated map and timeline
Locate and annotate a map showing places connected to First Nations Australians' songlines or cultural routes, alongside places personally connected to through family or community
elaborations: collecting information from sources and observations relevant to learning about the past (for example, photographs, interviews, newspapers, stories, and place and street names in maps) and relevant to learning about places (for example, surveying peers, satellite images, diagrams, field photographs, observations of monuments, built and non-built historical landmarks, middens, remnants of native vegetation and old building remains), and identifying relevant information
creating pictorial maps with annotations to show historical sites or places they are connected to, incorporating symbols to show locations of objects, places or significant features
locating the places they are connected to, such as through family, travel or friends, or the places they visit for shopping, recreation or other reasons on a print, electronic or wall map

ordering key events in the history of the local community or in its development using formats such as unscaled timelines, slideshows or stories; for example, the history of a person, place or building, or the developmental stages of telecommunications technologies

AC9HS2S03.minimum_width: Interpret distance or direction on one provided map using basic spatial terms.
AC9HS2S03.typical_width: Interpret geographic maps, concept maps and digital displays to explore spatial connections — including distance, accessibility and system relationships; interpret map symbols and legends; identify how objects and activities differ across local and distant places.
wider: Interpret how First Nations Australians' songlines connect places across a map, comparing this with a conventional transport or road map to identify what each type of spatial representation reveals
Interpret two different map types showing the same area (for example, a street map and an aerial photograph) and identify what can be determined from each
elaborations: interpreting distance on maps using terms such as "distant", "close", "local", "many hours in a bus/car/plane" and "walking distance" to decide on the accessibility of different features and places

interpreting geographic maps, concept maps and other digital or visual displays to explore system connections; for example, places their classmates are connected to, where some food comes from, how First Nations Australians' songlines connect places
interpreting symbols and codes that provide information, such as map legends
identifying how objects and activities are similar or different depending on conditions in local and distant places; for example, clothes, transport, technology

AC9HS2S04.minimum_width: Discuss why one place is considered special or significant by at least two different people or groups.
AC9HS2S04.typical_width: Discuss perspectives on special places and changes over time held by older generations, different cultural groups and community members; examine how the same place can be significant to different groups for different reasons.
wider: Explore how the same urban place holds different significance for First Nations Australians (for example, a traditional meeting place) and other cultural groups (for example, a monument or public building), examining how multiple layers of significance can coexist
Compare how First Nations Australians' and non-Indigenous Australians' perspectives on a changed local environment differ, identifying what shapes those different views
elaborations: discussing why some places are considered special or significant by others, such as parents, First Nations Australians, grandparents or familiar elders, friends and returned soldiers
examining the points of view of older generations about changes over time; for example, changes to the natural or built environment, changes to daily living

exploring how the same place has significance to different groups for different reasons; for example, traditional meeting places for First Nations Australians within an urban area that include buildings or monuments that are important to other cultural groups.

AC9HS2S05.minimum_width: Draw one conclusion about how a local place or technology has changed over time, supported by collected information.
AC9HS2S05.typical_width: Draw conclusions about local significance, continuity and change in technology, and spatial connections using Venn diagrams, tables or discussion; identify how change in one aspect of technology impacted life more broadly.
wider: Develop a future scenario for a local place, comparing a probable future with a preferred future and identifying specific actions that could influence which future eventuates
Use knowledge of a local natural system to draw conclusions about how human behaviour affects it — and what changes to behaviour could preserve its significance
elaborations: listing what makes a local person, place or building significant and drawing conclusions about how people were, or are, connected to a local place and other places in the region and/or state/territory
creating a Venn diagram or table that shows aspects of continuity or change in the local area or technology over time
discussing how change in one aspect of technology impacted on the way people worked, travelled, communicated or played in the past
identifying how knowledge of special places and natural systems in their local area contributes to behaviour, and ideas about how to care for these places and to preserve their significance
using their knowledge about a familiar place or site to imagine how it might change in the future and how they can influence a positive future for it

AC9HS2S06.minimum_width: Develop one short narrative about the past or share one observation about a place, using at least one subject-specific time term.
AC9HS2S06.typical_width: Develop narratives drawing on source comparisons; share observations about how a place has changed; use time terms (in the past, years ago, the olden days, in the future) and location terms (north, south, near, far) correctly.
wider: Present findings using both time and location terms together, situating a narrative in both its temporal and spatial context
Share narratives with a family member or community audience (not only to classmates) explaining what has been learned about a local place or period from the past
elaborations: developing narratives drawing on ideas in sources, such as a comparison of past and present daily life
sharing observations using sources such as how access to and use of a place has changed over time

sharing with their teacher, other students and members of their family what they know about the past, using terms in speech and writing to denote the passing of time (for example, "in the past", "years ago", "the olden days", "in the future") and to describe direction and location of a place (for example, "north", "south", "opposite", "near", "far")
